description.en: Sorting a million numbers to keep the best five is mostly wasted work. See how a small heap finds the top K with a fraction of the comparisons — and count them for real.

story_variants.en:
## You Only Wanted Five

"Show the top 5 scores." The obvious code is `sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:5]`. It is correct, short, and does far more work than the question needs: it puts **every** score in order, then throws almost all of that ordering away.

When K is small and N is large, there is a cheaper way. Keep a tiny **heap** of the best K seen so far. Each new score is compared against the *weakest* of those K; most scores lose that one comparison and are forgotten. Python packages this as `heapq.nlargest(k, items)` (and `nsmallest`).

```python
import heapq
heapq.nlargest(3, [41, 87, 15, 93, 62, 78, 30, 99, 54, 71])   # [99, 93, 87]
```

### Don't guess — count

We can measure the work without a stopwatch (timings change from machine to machine, counts don't). Wrap each number in a class whose `<` operator adds one to a counter, then run both approaches on the same 1,000 pseudo-random scores:

| Approach | Comparisons for top 5 of 1,000 |
|---|---|
| `sorted(...)[:5]` | 8,644 |
| `heapq.nlargest(5, ...)` | 1,073 |

With 10,000 scores the gap widens: 119,833 against 10,121. The heap's cost grows roughly in step with N (every item is looked at about once); a full sort grows like N log N.

### When it is *not* the right tool

- If K is close to N (say, half the data), `sorted` is simpler and about as fast.
- If you need the top 1, use `max(...)` — it is the K=1 case.
- If you need *all* the results ordered, you want a sort anyway.
- The heap approach changes nothing about the answer: ties and order match a full sort. Only the work differs.

> **Vaathiyaar's note:** the habit to build is asking *"how much of this ordering do I actually use?"* If the answer is "a few items", don't pay for the rest.

Your turn: `top_k` below sorts everything. Rewrite it so it passes the answer check **and** a comparison-count check on 1,000 scores.

explanation.en: Ten scores; we want the best three.
Start with the first K scores in a min-heap: heap[0] is the weakest of the current best.
A new score only matters if it beats the weakest of the K. Most don't, and cost one comparison.
Only K items remain, so ordering them at the end is cheap.

lines: comparisons, 1,000 scores, k=5: sorted 8,644 vs nlargest 1,073

instruction.en: `top_k(scores, k)` returns the k largest scores, largest first — but it sorts ALL of them. Rewrite it with the `heapq` module so it keeps only k items in play. A hidden check counts comparisons on 1,000 scores (a full sort takes about 8,600; yours must stay under 4,000) and also tries edge cases: k larger than the list, an empty list, k = 0 and ties. With the sample scores, the program must print `[99, 93, 87]`.

practice_challenges.starter_code:
def top_k(scores, k):
    """Return the k largest scores, largest first."""
    # This works, but it sorts ALL the scores just to keep k of them.
    return sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:k]

print(top_k([41, 87, 15, 93, 62, 78, 30, 99, 54, 71], 3))

en: `import heapq` — it has a ready-made `nlargest(k, iterable)`.
`heapq.nlargest(k, scores)` already returns the items largest first.
It handles k bigger than the list and an empty list for you.
Keep the signature `top_k(scores, k)` and the print at the bottom.

practice_challenges.test_code:
class _Counted:
    comparisons = 0
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
    def __lt__(self, other):
        _Counted.comparisons += 1
        return self.v < other.v

def _data(n):
    x, out = 12345, []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2**31
        out.append(x % 100000)
    return out

assert [int(v) for v in top_k([41, 87, 15, 93, 62, 78, 30, 99, 54, 71], 3)] == [99, 93, 87]
assert list(top_k([5, 1], 5)) == [5, 1]
assert list(top_k([], 3)) == []
assert list(top_k([4, 9, 9, 2], 2)) == [9, 9]
assert list(top_k([4, 9, 2], 0)) == []

_vals = _data(1000)
_items = [_Counted(v) for v in _vals]
_Counted.comparisons = 0
_got = top_k(_items, 5)
assert [c.v for c in _got] == sorted(_vals, reverse=True)[:5], "wrong answer on 1000 scores"
assert _Counted.comparisons < 4000, (
    f"{_Counted.comparisons} comparisons on 1000 scores: sorting everything costs about 8600; "
    "keep only k items in a heap instead")

q.en: Why is `sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:5]` wasteful on a million scores?

en: Python's sort is incorrect for large lists
It orders every score, then discards nearly all of that ordering
It cannot return fewer than all items
Slicing copies the whole list twice

q.en: In the lesson's count of 1,000 scores with k=5, roughly how many comparisons did `heapq.nlargest` need?

en: About 1,073
About 8,644
About 100,000
Exactly 5

q.en: Which call is the K=1 special case of the top-K problem?

en: `min(scores)`
`max(scores)`
`sorted(scores)[1]`
`len(scores)`

q.en: When is plain `sorted(...)` the better choice?

en: When K is tiny and N is huge
When you need most or all items in order
When the list is empty
Never — heaps are always faster

q.en: Why does the lesson count comparisons instead of timing the code?

en: Counting is more fun
Timings vary by machine and load; the count is the same every run
Python cannot measure time
Comparisons are the only cost in Python

under_the_hood.summary: Selecting the best K of N items does not need N items in order. A heap of size K keeps just the current best, so each item costs about one comparison instead of a full sort's log N.

steps.title: A full sort orders everything
steps.body: `sorted` runs Timsort over all N items. That takes on the order of N log N comparisons, because every item must end up in its exact position — even the ones you will throw away right after taking `[:k]`.

left.label: sorted(...)[:5]
left.code: sorted(items)\n# every item placed\n# ~8,644 comparisons for N=1,000

right.label: heapq.nlargest(5, items)
right.code: heap of 5\n# most items lose 1 test\n# ~1,073 comparisons for N=1,000

steps.title: A heap keeps the weakest on top
steps.body: A min-heap is a list arranged so `heap[0]` is always the smallest item. If the heap holds the K best so far, `heap[0]` is the *weakest of the best* — the bar a newcomer has to clear. Reading it costs nothing.

steps.title: Each new item makes one test
steps.body: For each remaining item, compare it with `heap[0]`. If it is not larger, drop it: one comparison, done. If it is larger, swap it in and let it sink to its place, which costs about log K more steps — but this becomes rare as the heap fills with strong items.

steps.title: Finish by ordering only K items
steps.body: After the pass the heap holds exactly the K winners, unordered. Sorting those K items at the end costs K log K — tiny when K is small. `nlargest` does this for you and returns them largest first.

steps.title: Why counting beats timing here
steps.body: Wall-clock times shift with the machine, other programs and caching. A counter inside `__lt__` gives the same number every run, so it shows the *algorithmic* difference and cannot be blamed on noise. Real code should still be timed too — see the measuring lesson.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Ask how much of the ordering you actually use. If you want a handful of winners out of a large pile, a size-K heap does about N work instead of N log N, with an identical answer.
